property_summary: For any caller who is the owner and any starting contract balance, calling withdrawAll transfers the entire contract balance to the owner (leaving address(c).balance == 0); the mutant that only withdraws half breaks this rule for some balances.

For any owner and any initial contract balance > 0, calling withdrawAll empties the contract (address(c).balance == 0); the mutant that withdraws only half leaves a nonzero balance for some initial balances, breaking this rule.

For any owner caller and any initial contract balance that is an exact even number of wei (i.e., balance % 2 == 0), calling withdrawAll transfers the entire balance away so that address(c).balance == 0; the mutant that withdraws only half leaves a non-zero balance for such even balances and thus violates the rule for some inputs.

For any owner caller and any initial contract balance B, calling withdrawAll results in the owner's received increase equaling B (i.e., owner's balance after minus before equals address(c).balance_before); the mutant that withdraws half breaks this because the owner only receives B/2 for some B.

For any owner caller and any initial contract balance that is exactly 1 wei, calling withdrawAll transfers that 1 wei to the owner so that address(c).balance == 0; the mutant that withdraws half (0 wei) leaves balance 1 and thus violates this rule for that input.

For any caller and any amount <= contract balance, calling withdraw(...) by the owner always results in the full requested amount being sent (withdraw succeeds); the mutant using send can fail to deliver the amount when the recipient is a contract whose fallback/receive reverts, causing withdraw to revert or behave differently.

For any recipient contract and any withdraw amount, the reference contract always transfers the requested ETH to the caller (using transfer which reverts on failure), whereas the mutant replaced transfer with send which can fail silently (returning false) causing the call to revert or deliver different post-state for some recipient contracts; thus: calling withdraw(amount) as owner always results in address(c).balance decreasing by amount in the reference, while the mutant can fail to do so for some recipient behavior.

For any owner-invoked withdraw(amount) the reference contract always forwards the requested ETH out (so address(c).balance decreases by exactly amount); replacing transfer with send can fail when the recipient reverts on receive/fallback, so for some recipient contracts the mutant will not decrease address(c).balance by the requested amount.

For any owner-invoked withdraw(amount) where the caller is a contract whose fallback reverts, the reference C (which uses transfer) will revert and thus not change address(c).balance only when the transfer itself reverts; the mutant using send can return false causing withdraw to revert as well — we assert that calling withdraw as the owner always either successfully sends the requested amount (decreasing address(c).balance by amount) or reverts; specifically, for the reference, invoking withdraw(amount) from the owner-contract that reverts on receive will cause the call to revert (ok == false) for some amounts/conditions that the mutant mishandles, so we assert behavior observed via a try/catch on withdraw succeeds for the reference across inputs while the mutant fails for some inputs.

For every uint amount the owner withdraws, the reference contract always either (1) successfully sends that exact amount out (reducing address(c).balance by amount) or (2) reverts; the mutant using send can return false in some cases and cause withdraw to revert while the reference would have succeeded (i.e., there exist amounts and recipient behaviors where the post-call contract balance differs between reference and mutant).

Rule: withdraw(amount) always reduces the contract balance by exactly amount (succeeds and sends funds) for the reference (which uses transfer that reverts on failure), whereas replacing transfer with a low-level call can succeed/fail differently when the recipient reverts in its fallback — the mutant can cause withdraw to revert or behave differently for some recipient fallback behavior.

For any recipient contract, a withdraw(amount) call from the owner always transfers the requested amount out of C (reducing address(c).balance by exactly amount) because transfer reverts on failure; replacing transfer with a low-level call can observe a reverting recipient and thus cause the operation to fail or behave differently for some recipient/fallback, breaking that invariant.

For any owner-triggered withdraw(amount) to a recipient contract whose fallback reverts, the reference C (which uses transfer) will always revert the withdraw (so the call does not succeed) and leave c.balance unchanged; replacing transfer with a low-level call that forwards all gas can allow the withdraw to succeed (or at least behave differently) for some inputs—so the mutant changes whether withdraw reverts against a reverting recipient.

For any recipient contract whose fallback consumes more than 2300 gas (causing transfer to revert), C.withdraw(amount) (called by owner) always REVERTS and thus leaves address(c).balance unchanged; replacing transfer with a .call that forwards all gas can allow the call to succeed (or at least not revert) for some such recipient, so the mutant does not revert in those cases.

For any recipient contract with a fallback that REVERTS, calling withdraw(amount) as owner always reverts on the reference (so c.balance remains unchanged); the mutant using call{value:...}("") can instead return false (or behave differently) causing withdraw to NOT revert and therefore change c.balance — the test asserts that withdraw to a reverting recipient always reverts (reference true for all inputs, mutant false for some).

Rule: Only the owner can successfully call withdraw (calls from non-owners revert or fail); the mutant inverts the check allowing non-owners and preventing the owner, so some input (a call from the original owner) will behave differently (succeed on reference vs fail on mutant or vice versa).

For every caller address and amount, the original contract allows the owner (deployer) to successfully call withdraw and transfer funds, while the mutant inverts the onlyOwner check and prevents the original owner from withdrawing (so a call to withdraw by the deployer that succeeds on the reference will fail on the mutant for some fuzzed amount).

For every caller address and withdrawal amount, the deploying owner (the contract's owner) can always successfully call withdraw(amount) on the reference contract (the call does not revert and transfers funds if available); the mutant inverts the onlyOwner check so the owner's withdraw calls can revert for some admissible inputs, causing a difference.

For any caller address and amount, the deployer (owner) can always successfully call withdraw(amount) (call returns/does not revert) on the reference contract C; the mutant inverts onlyOwner so the deployer's withdraw call will revert (fail) for some inputs, so the behavior differs.

For any caller address and uint amount, calling withdraw on C by the contract owner (deployer) always succeeds (does not revert) and returns control; the mutant that inverts onlyOwner will make the owner's withdraw revert (fail) for some inputs — so the universal property is: owner withdraw never reverts on the reference.

For any caller and any value v that the contract holds, only the owner can withdraw funds so after any withdraw attempt by an arbitrary caller the contract balance remains unchanged (unless caller is owner); the mutant removes onlyOwner allowing non-owners to drain funds, violating this rule for some caller/value.

For any caller and amount, when the owner calls sendMoney(target, value, data) sending value wei, the contract's balance decreases by exactly value and the recipient is the external target (i.e., address(this).balance == oldBalance - value); the mutant redirects funds to msg.sender causing address(this).balance to not decrease by value when target would have received it.

For any target contract that rejects received funds (reverts in its fallback/receive), the correct C.sendMoney(...) must revert (because it requires the low-level call to succeed), whereas the mutant that transfers to msg.sender will succeed; thus for all admissible inputs the reference reverts (ok == false) but the mutant allows ok == true for some inputs.

For any callee contract that accepts payable calls and forwards/re-uses funds, calling sendMoney(target, value, data) from the owner always results in the target's balance increasing by exactly value (reference preserves recipient = target); the mutant that transfers to msg.sender breaks this because the target's balance will not increase for some inputs.

For every target address and value, when the owner calls sendMoney(target, value, data) the reference contract always reduces its own balance by exactly value (funds leave the contract), but the mutant that transfers to msg.sender can leave the contract balance unchanged for some inputs, so the rule 'address(c).balance decreases by value after sendMoney' holds for the reference and is violated by the mutant for some inputs.

When the owner calls sendMoney(target, value, data) the reference contract always leaves the caller (owner) balance unchanged (it sends funds to the specified target), whereas the mutant redirects funds to the caller so the owner's balance increases for some inputs — therefore: for all admissible inputs, after sendMoney the owner's balance equals its prior balance (reference); the mutant can make it larger.
